source: Marqu - The Hebrew Gospel of Mark v1.2
notes_on_source: Verse 37 is missing from the source (jumps from v36 to v38).

verses.translation: And in those other times a great{H7227} host{H2428} of people{H5971} gathered{H622} with Yeshua, and they had nothing to eat{H398}. And he called{H7121} his disciples and said{H559} to them:

one_way_hebrew: Uses חיל (chayil, H2428 — 'host/army/force'). This is the OT word for military strength, wealth, and force (Ex 14:4, Deut 8:17, Josh 1:14, Ruth 2:1 'mighty man of chayil'). Greek has ὄχλου πολλοῦ ('great crowd'). A back-translator from 'crowd' would use המון (hamon — 'multitude') or קהל (qahal — 'assembly'), not the military-wealth term חיל. The Hebrew frames the crowd as an 'army' — a host gathered around their commander.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'a great host of people' (חיל — military/force). Greek: 'a very great multitude' (ὄχλου πολλοῦ — neutral crowd).

verses.translation: I have compassion{H7356} upon the people{H5971}, for they have been following{H4900} after me these three{H7969} days{H3117} and have nothing to eat{H398}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses רחמנות (rachmanut — 'compassion', from רחם H7356 — 'womb'). This is the visceral, maternal compassion — womb-love. Greek has σπλαγχνίζομαι ('moved in the bowels/intestines'). Both use visceral metaphors but from different body organs: Hebrew from the womb (feminine/maternal); Greek from the intestines (gender-neutral). A back-translator from Greek intestinal compassion would not independently choose the womb-compassion word.

verses.translation: And if I send{H7971} them to their houses{H1004} they will faint{H5848} on the way{H1870}, for some of them have come{H935} from afar{H7350}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יתעלפו (yit'alefu — 'they will faint/swoon'). The root עלף appears in the OT for fainting/swooning (Isa 51:20, Amos 8:13, Jonah 4:8). Greek has ἐκλυθήσονται ('they will give out/collapse'). A back-translator would use יפלו (yiplu — 'they will fall') or ייעפו (yi'afu — 'they will tire'). The Hebrew verb carries overtones of heat exhaustion and physical collapse.

verses.translation: And the disciples answered{H6030}: From what food{H3978} could this people{H5971} be satisfied{H7646} in the wilderness{H4057}?

one_way_hebrew: The phrase 'satisfied in the wilderness' (לשבוע...במדבר) directly invokes the manna narrative. שבע (sava — 'satisfied', H7646) + מדבר (midbar — 'wilderness', H4057) together echo Deuteronomy 8:15-16: 'who led you through the great and terrifying wilderness... who fed you with manna in the wilderness.' The disciples' question is framed in Exodus language — where will bread come from in the wilderness?
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 8:15-16: the manna feeding in the wilderness. The disciples fail to connect Yeshua's first feeding (ch. 6) with the wilderness provision pattern.

verses.translation: And Yeshua asked{H7592} them: How many loaves{H3603} of bread{H3899} do you have? And they answered{H6030}: Seven.

And he commanded{H6680} the people{H5971} to sit{H3427} on the ground{H776}, and took{H3947} the seven{H7651} loaves{H3899}, making supplications{H2580}, and broke{H7665} them and gave{H5414} them to his disciples and said{H559} to them: Set{H5117} them before the people{H5971}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חנות (chanot — 'supplications/grace-seeking', from חן H2580 — 'grace'). Greek has εὐχαριστήσας ('having given thanks'). In the first feeding (6:41), the Hebrew had חינות והודאות ('supplications and thanksgivings'). Here only חנות — the grace-petition. A back-translator from Greek 'gave thanks' would use הודה (hodah — 'thanked'), not the grace-supplication verb.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'making supplications' (חנות — seeking grace). Greek: 'gave thanks' (εὐχαριστέω). Different liturgical acts.

verses.translation: And they had a few{H4592} fish{H1709}; he blessed{H1288} them and commanded{H6680}: Set{H5117} them before them.
And they and all{H3605} the people{H5971} ate{H398} and were satisfied{H7646}. Afterward they collected{H5493} from the remainder{H3498} seven{H7651} full{H4392} baskets.

translation_notes: Seven full baskets remaining — seven may symbolize divine completeness, contrasting with the twelve baskets of the first feeding (representing the twelve tribes).

verses.translation: And those who ate{H398} were about four{H702} thousand{H505} men{H376}. And he released them to go{H1980}.
And immediately Yeshua went up{H5927} in a ship{H5600} with his disciples and came{H935} to Kfar Nachum and Dalmanuta.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew preserves כפר נחום (Kfar Nachum — 'Village of Consolation/Nahum'). Greek has εἰς τὰ μέρη Δαλμανουθά ('to the region of Dalmanutha'). The Hebrew includes a specific destination (Kfar Nachum) that Greek lacks in this verse. The Hebrew place-name is meaningful: 'Village of Comfort' (from נחם — 'to comfort').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Kfar Nachum and Dalmanuta' (two destinations). Greek: 'the region of Dalmanutha' (one destination). Hebrew includes Kfar Nachum.

verses.translation: And the Separatists{H6504} went out{H3318} and debated{H3198} with them and tested{H5254} him, asking{H7592} for a sign{H226} from the heavens{H8064}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אות (ot, H226 — 'sign/omen/miraculous sign'). This is the OT word for God's signs: the rainbow (Gen 9:12), circumcision (Gen 17:11), the Exodus signs (Ex 4:8, 7:3, Deut 4:34). Greek has σημεῖον ('sign'). While similar in meaning, the Hebrew carries the full weight of OT sign-theology. The Pharisees demand an 'ot' — the kind of sign God gave Moses.

Uses נתוכחו (nitvakhechu — 'debated/argued', from יכח H3198 — 'to reprove/argue/reason'). This is the prophetic confrontation verb (Isa 1:18 'Come, let us reason together'; Job 13:3, 23:7). Greek has ἤρξαντο συζητεῖν ('began to dispute'). A back-translator would use התווכחו (hitvakhechu) or similar, but the Hebrew verb specifically invokes prophetic argumentation.

verses.translation: And Yeshua said{H559} to them: Truly{H571} I say{H559} to you that you shall not see{H7200} a sign{H226} of visions.

one_way_hebrew: Uses סימן ההראות (siman ha-hera'ot — 'a sign of visions/showings'). This compound phrase means 'a visionary sign' — a sign that comes through divine vision. Greek has σημεῖον ('a sign'). The Hebrew is more specific: not just any sign, but a sign of prophetic vision. A back-translator from Greek would write simply אות ('sign'), not this elaborate visionary construction.

Uses אמת (emet, H571 — 'truth') where Greek has ἀμὴν (amēn — a Hebrew loanword transliterated). The Hebrew uses 'truth' as the introductory formula; the Greek transliterates the Hebrew אמן ('amen'). The Hebrew author says 'truth' (אמת); the Greek converts it to the liturgical 'amen.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'truly' (אמת — truth). Greek: 'amen' (ἀμήν — transliterated Hebrew). Different forms.
Hebrew: 'a sign of visions' (elaborate). Greek: 'a sign' (simple). Hebrew is more specific.

verses.translation: And he left{H5800} them and went up{H5927} in a ship{H5600}, crossing{H5674} to the other side of the sea{H3220}.
And his disciples forgot{H7911} to take{H3947} bread{H3899}, and they had only one{H259} loaf{H3899}.
And he warned{H2094} them, saying{H559}: See{H7200}! Guard{H8104} yourselves from the leaven{H7603} of the Separatists{H6504} and of Herodos.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שאור (se'or, H7603 — 'leaven/sourdough'). This is the specific OT word for the leaven forbidden during Pesach (Ex 12:15,19, 13:7). Greek has ζύμη ('leaven'). While the meanings overlap, the Hebrew שאור specifically evokes the Passover prohibition — leaven as moral/spiritual contamination that must be purged. The Pesach context is immediate in Hebrew; in Greek it's merely metaphorical.
textual_notes: Exodus 12:15: 'Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread. On the first day you shall remove leaven (שאור) from your houses.' The Passover leaven purge is the background for Yeshua's warning.

verses.translation: And they, thinking{H2803}, said{H559} one to another: He said this because we have no bread{H3899}.
And Yeshua, when he saw{H7200} their thoughts{H4284}, said{H559} to them: Still{H5750} you do not recognize{H5234} nor understand{H995}? Still{H5750} is your heart{H3824} blind{H5787}?

one_way_hebrew: Uses עור לבבכם (iver levavkhem — 'blind is your heart', with עור H5787 — 'blind'). Greek has πεπωρωμένην... τὴν καρδίαν ('hardened heart'). In Mark 6:52, the Hebrew used ערפליי ('clouded'). Now it escalates to 'blind.' A back-translator from 'hardened' would use מוקשה (muqshah) or ערל (arel — 'uncircumcised/blocked'), not עור ('blind'). The Hebrew says the heart has eyes that have gone blind — a different metaphor from hardening.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'blind heart' (עור — visual metaphor). Greek: 'hardened heart' (πεπωρωμένη — petrification metaphor). Different images.

verses.translation: Eyes{H5869} you have and you do not see{H7200}; ears{H241} you have and you do not hear{H8085}. Have you no memory{H2146}?

one_way_hebrew: VERBATIM OT QUOTATION: 'Eyes you have and do not see, ears you have and do not hear' — from Jeremiah 5:21 (עינים להם ולא יראו אזנים להם ולא ישמעו) and Ezekiel 12:2 (עינים להם לראות ולא ראו אזנים להם לשמע ולא שמעו). Also Deuteronomy 29:3 and Psalm 115:5-6 / 135:16-17. The Hebrew preserves the prophetic source text. Greek renders it as a translation. The Hebrew IS the source.

Adds אין לכם זכרון (ein lakhem zikaron — 'have you no memory/memorial?'). The word זכרון (zikaron, H2146) is the OT word for memorial/remembrance — the same word used for Passover (Ex 12:14 'this day shall be for you a memorial/zikaron') and the memorial stones of Joshua 4:7. Greek has οὐ μνημονεύετε ('do you not remember?'). The Hebrew asks about zikaron — the covenantal, liturgical act of remembrance.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'have you no memorial/remembrance?' (זכרון — covenantal memory). Greek: 'do you not remember?' (μνημονεύω — recall).
textual_notes: Jeremiah 5:21: 'Hear this, O foolish people without understanding, who have eyes and see not, who have ears and hear not.' Yeshua applies the prophetic rebuke of Israel to his own disciples.

verses.translation: When I divided{H2505} the five{H2568} loaves{H3899} to the five{H2568} thousand{H505} men{H376}, how many{H4100} baskets remained{H7604} of the surplus? And they said{H559}: Twelve{H8147}{H6240}.
And of the seven{H7651} loaves{H3899} to the four{H702} thousand{H505} men{H376}, how many{H4100} baskets remained{H7604}? And they said{H559}: Seven{H7651}.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew uses two different words for 'basket': קופות (qufot) in v19 and סלים (salim, H5536) in v20. Greek also distinguishes: κοφίνων (large wicker baskets) in v19 and σπυρίδων (flexible hampers) in v20. Both Hebrew and Greek preserve a distinction between the two feeding miracles' baskets — suggesting independent witnesses to the same detail, not translation.
translation_notes: The two different basket words in both Hebrew and Greek independently preserve the same distinction between the two feedings.

verses.translation: And he said{H559} to them: If so, do you not understand{H995}?
And they came{H935} to Beit Tsaidah, and they brought{H1980} to him one{H259} man{H376} who was blind{H5787}, and they begged{H1245} him to touch{H5060} him.

translation_notes: בית צידה (Beit Tsaidah) — 'House of Hunting/Fishing.' The Hebrew preserves the Semitic meaning.

verses.translation: And Yeshua took{H3947} him by the hand{H3027} and drew{H4900} him aside{H6654} from the path{H1870}, and spat{H7556} on his face{H6440} and laid{H5117} his hands{H3027} upon him and asked{H7592} him if he saw{H7200}.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew: 'spat on his face' (רקק לו בפניו). Greek: 'spit on his eyes' (πτύσας εἰς τὰ ὄμματα). Different target: face (פנים) vs. eyes (ὄμματα). The Hebrew is broader; the Greek more specific.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'on his face' (בפניו). Greek: 'on his eyes' (εἰς τὰ ὄμματα). Different target.

verses.translation: And he looked{H5027} and said{H559}: I see{H7200} the peoples{H5971} walking{H1980}, upright like trees{H6086}.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew says 'I see the walking of the peoples, upright like trees' (הלוך העמים זקופים כמו אילנות). Greek says ὅτι ὡς δένδρα ὁρῶ περιπατοῦντας ('I see men walking like trees'). The Hebrew structure is different: he sees the peoples' movement, then describes them as upright like trees. The word זקופים (zequfim — 'upright/erect') emphasizes their vertical posture. The Hebrew perspective is more dynamic — he perceives movement and uprightness.

verses.translation: And again he laid{H5117} his hands{H3027} on his eyes{H5869}, and he began to see{H7200} with clarity.

textual_notes: The two-stage healing is unique in the Gospels. It may symbolize the disciples' partial understanding — they see, but not yet clearly (cf. vv17-21).

verses.translation: And Yeshua sent{H7971} him to his house{H1004}, saying{H559} to him: Do not tell{H559} any man{H120} among your neighbors{H7934}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses משכיניך (mi-shekhenaikha — 'among your neighbors', from שכן H7934 — 'neighbor/one who dwells near'). Greek has μηδὲ εἰς τὴν κώμην εἰσέλθῃς ('do not enter into the village'). Completely different instructions: the Hebrew says don't tell your neighbors; the Greek says don't enter the village. A back-translator would not convert 'don't enter the village' into 'don't tell your neighbors.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'do not tell any man among your neighbors.' Greek: 'do not enter the village.' Different commands.

verses.translation: And yet{H5750} Yeshua asked{H7592} his disciples: What do the peoples{H5971} say{H559} of me — who am I?
And they answered{H6030}, saying{H559}: You are Yochanan{H3110} the Immerser{H2881}. And others say{H559} Eliyahu{H452}. And some say{H559} a prophet{H5030}.
And he said{H559} to them: And you — what do you say{H559} of me? Who am I? And Keyfa answered{H6030} and said{H559}: You are Mashiach{H4899}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses משיח (Mashiach, H4899 — 'the Anointed One'). This is the OT title for the anointed king (1 Sam 2:10, 24:7, 2 Sam 22:51, Ps 2:2) and the prophesied deliverer (Dan 9:25-26). Greek has ὁ Χριστός ('the Christ'). While Christos is the standard Greek translation of Mashiach, the Hebrew carries the full OT anointing theology — the oil poured on kings (1 Sam 10:1, 16:13) and priests (Ex 28:41). The Hebrew title is the original; the Greek is the translation.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: simply 'Mashiach' (the Anointed One). Greek adds τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ζῶντος ('of the living God') in Matthew's parallel, but Mark's Greek also has just ὁ Χριστός.
textual_notes: Psalm 2:2: 'The kings of the earth set themselves... against YHWH and against his Anointed One (משיחו).' Keyfa's confession identifies Yeshua with the Psalm 2 king.

verses.translation: Therefore he commanded{H6680} them that they should not make it known{H6942}.

Saying{H559} and showing{H7200} and teaching{H3925} that he must suffer{H5375} pain{H6862} and be pushed to death{H4194} by the chief{H8269} priests{H3548} and the wise-men of the religion{H1881}; and he shall rise{H6965} alive{H2416} after three{H7969} days{H3117}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נגוש (nagush — 'pushed/pressed/driven', from נגש H5065 — 'to oppress/drive/exact'). This is the word for the Egyptian taskmasters oppressing Israel (Ex 3:7, 5:6,10,13,14; Isa 3:12). Greek has ἀποδοκιμασθῆναι ('to be rejected'). A back-translator from 'rejected' would use נמאס (nim'as — 'rejected') or נדחה (nidchah — 'pushed away'). The Hebrew says Yeshua will be 'oppressed' like Israel in Egypt — an Exodus-suffering verb.

Uses שרי הכהנים (sarei ha-kohanim — 'officers/princes of the priests') and חכמי הדת (chakhmei ha-dat — 'wise-men of the religion'). Greek has ἀρχιερέων ('chief priests') and γραμματέων ('scribes'). The Hebrew uses different institutional titles throughout — never importing Greek terminology.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'pushed/oppressed to death' (נגש — Exodus oppression). Greek: 'rejected' (ἀποδοκιμάζω — official disapproval). Different verbs.
Hebrew: 'officers of the priests' and 'wise-men of the religion.' Greek: 'chief priests' and 'scribes.' Different titles.
textual_notes: Isaiah 53:7: 'He was oppressed (נגש) and he was afflicted.' The same verb נגש connects Yeshua's suffering prediction to Isaiah's Suffering Servant.

verses.translation: And he said{H559} these things openly{H1540}. And Keyfa began to rebuke{H1605} him.

And Yeshua turned{H2015} before{H6440} the disciples, rebuking{H1605} Keyfa, and said{H559}: Depart{H6504} from me, O adversary{H7854}! For you have no understanding{H7922} divine{H430}, but fleshly{H1320}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses שכנגדי (she-kenegdi — 'that which is against me/my adversary'). This is formed from כנגד (keneged — 'opposite/against/corresponding to'). The same root appears in Genesis 2:18 where God makes an עזר כנגדו (ezer kenegdo — 'a helper corresponding to him') for Adam. Greek has Σατανᾶ ('Satan'). A back-translator from 'Satan' would simply write שטן. The Hebrew does NOT use שטן here but a phrase meaning 'my adversary/opponent' — describing the ROLE (one who opposes), not the TITLE (Satan).

Uses שכל אלהיי...בשריי (sekhel elohiy...basriy — 'divine understanding...fleshly'). The contrast is between אלהיי (from אלהים — 'divine/of God') and בשריי (from בשר — 'flesh/carnal'). Greek has τὰ τοῦ θεοῦ... τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ('the things of God... the things of men'). The Hebrew pairs divine understanding (שכל) with fleshly thinking — the contrast is intellectual/spiritual. The Greek pairs God's things with men's things — a more abstract contrast.

Uses הפרד (hipared — 'separate yourself/depart', from פרד H6504 — 'to separate'). This is the root of the Pharisees' name (פרושים — 'the separated'). Greek has ὕπαγε ('go away/get behind'). Yeshua tells Keyfa to 'separate' — ironically using the Pharisaic root. He becomes a 'Pharisee' (separator) by thinking fleshly thoughts.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'my adversary' (שכנגדי — descriptive). Greek: 'Satan' (Σατανᾶ — title/name). Different handling of the rebuke.
Hebrew: 'no divine understanding, but fleshly' (intellectual contrast). Greek: 'not minding God's things, but men's things' (orientation contrast).
Hebrew: 'depart/separate' (הפרד — same root as 'Pharisee'). Greek: 'get behind' (ὕπαγε).
translation_notes: 'Adversary' for she-kenegdi rather than 'Satan' — the Hebrew describes a role, not a title. Keyfa acts as an adversary to the divine plan, not as THE Satan.
The ironic use of הפרד (Pharisee-root) against Keyfa: 'Separate yourself from me' — you who oppose God's plan have become a Separator.

verses.translation: And he called{H7121} the people{H5971} and his disciples and said{H559} to them: The one who wishes{H7521} to follow{H4900} after me — let him deny{H3584} himself and take{H3947} his warp-and-woof with him, and follow{H4900} after me.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses שתי וערב (sheti va-erev — 'warp and woof'). These are the two sets of threads in weaving: the vertical (warp/שתי) and the horizontal (woof/ערב). Together they form the CROSS pattern of woven fabric. Greek has σταυρόν ('cross' — the Roman execution instrument). A back-translator from Greek σταυρός would use צלב (tselav — 'cross') or עמוד (amud — 'stake/post'). NO back-translator would EVER independently generate 'warp and woof' from 'cross.' This is one of the most extraordinary one-way markers in the Hebrew Gospels.

The phrase שתי וערב appears in Leviticus 13:48,49,51,52,53,56,57,58,59 as part of the laws of צרעת (tsara'at — 'leprosy/skin disease') in garments. The priest inspects the שתי או בערב ('warp or woof') for signs of disease. The warp-and-woof is connected to ritual purity examination. The Hebrew says: take your warp-and-woof (the place where impurity is found and examined) and follow me — a purification metaphor that only works in Hebrew/Levitical context.

Uses יכפור (yikhpor — 'let him deny/disavow', from כפר H3584 — 'to deny/lie/disown'). This root also means 'to cover/atone' (כפר, kaphar). The wordplay: deny (כפר) yourself = atone (כפר) for yourself. This double meaning only works in Hebrew.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'warp and woof' (שתי וערב — weaving/Levitical purity). Greek: 'cross' (σταυρός — Roman execution). Entirely different imagery with utterly different cultural contexts.
Hebrew: 'deny' (כפר — also 'atone'). Greek: 'deny' (ἀπαρνέομαι — renounce). Hebrew has double meaning.
translation_notes: 'Warp-and-woof' for sheti va-erev — the intersecting threads of a loom. The cross-shape is inherent in the weaving: vertical threads crossed by horizontal threads. The Hebrew preserves the original metaphor from which the Greek 'cross' derives its meaning in this context.

The Leviticus 13 connection: שתי וערב is the location in fabric where impurity manifests and must be examined by a priest. To 'take up your warp-and-woof' is to carry the site of impurity examination — to bear one's own purification.
textual_notes: Leviticus 13:48: 'whether in the warp (שתי) or the woof (ערב)... it is a leprous disease.' The warp-and-woof is where spiritual disease is diagnosed. Yeshua transforms the image: carry your warp-and-woof (the cross-pattern where sin is diagnosed and purged) and follow me.

verses.translation: And whoever wishes{H2654} to make{H6213} his soul{H5315} saved{H3467} shall lose{H6} it, and the one who loses{H6} it for my sake and for the sake of the good-news{H1319} shall save{H3467} it.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הבשורה (ha-besorah — 'the good-news', from בשר H1319 — 'to bring good tidings'). This is the specific OT word for joyful proclamation: Isaiah 40:9 ('O bearer of good tidings to Zion'), 52:7 ('How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good tidings'), 61:1 ('YHWH has anointed me to bring good tidings'). Greek has εὐαγγέλιον ('gospel/good news'). While etymologically parallel, the Hebrew word carries the specific Isaiah context of messianic proclamation.
Again uses ישע (yasha, H3467 — 'to save') — the root of Yeshua's name. The wordplay: 'whoever loses his soul for Yeshua (ישוע) shall save (יושיע) it.' The salvation is embedded in the Savior's name.
translation_notes: 'Good-news' for besorah — preserving the Isaiah herald-proclamation sense rather than importing the ecclesiastical 'gospel.'
textual_notes: Isaiah 52:7: 'How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good tidings (מבשר), who publishes peace, who brings good tidings of good.' The besorah is the messianic herald's message.

verses.translation: And what does it profit{H3276} a man{H120} even{H1571} if he has all{H3605} the world{H8398} and loses{H6} his soul{H5315}?

translation_notes: Uses both נשמה (neshamah, v35 — 'breath-soul', the divine breath of Gen 2:7) and נפש (nefesh, v36 — 'living soul/life-force'). Hebrew distinguishes between these; Greek uses ψυχή for both.

verses.translation: And the one who acknowledges{H5234} me and proclaims{H6942} me and my words{H1697} in this adulterous{H5003}, sinful{H2399} nation{H524} — the Son{H1121} of the Virgin{H1330} shall acknowledge{H5234} him before HaShem{H8034} the Father{H1} when he comes{H935} in his light{H216} with the messengers{H4397}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בן הבתולה (ben ha-betulah — 'the Son of the Virgin', H1121 + H1330). Greek has ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ('the Son of Man'). A back-translator from Greek 'Son of Man' would write בן אדם (ben adam) or בן אנוש (ben enosh) — the Daniel 7:13 title. The Hebrew says 'SON OF THE VIRGIN' — a completely different title that directly invokes Isaiah 7:14 (הנה הבתולה הרה וילדת בן — 'behold, the virgin is with child and bears a son'). This is among the most striking one-way markers in the entire Hebrew Gospels. No back-translator from Greek would EVER replace 'Son of Man' with 'Son of the Virgin.'

Uses האומה מנאפת חטאה ('this adulterous, sinful nation'). Hebrew uses אומה (ummah, H524 — 'nation/tribe') rather than the Greek γενεά ('generation'). A back-translator from 'generation' would use דור (dor — 'generation'). The Hebrew אומה implies a national entity, not a temporal generation.

Uses באורו (be-oro — 'in his light', from אור H216 — 'light'). Greek has ἐν τῇ δόξῃ τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτοῦ ('in the glory of his Father'). Hebrew: 'in his light.' Greek: 'in glory.' A back-translator from 'glory' would use בכבודו (be-khvodo), not באורו. Light (אור) is a more primordial divine attribute (Gen 1:3 'Let there be light') than glory (כבוד).
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew: 'Son of the Virgin' (בן הבתולה — Isaiah 7:14). Greek: 'Son of Man' (υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου — Daniel 7:13). Completely different Christological titles.
Hebrew: 'this adulterous, sinful nation' (אומה — national entity). Greek: 'this adulterous and sinful generation' (γενεά — temporal generation).
Hebrew: 'in his light' (אור — primordial light). Greek: 'in the glory of his Father' (δόξα — glory). Different divine attributes.
Hebrew: 'HaShem the Father' (השם האב). Greek: 'his Father' (τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτοῦ). Hebrew uses the divine Name circumlocution.
translation_notes: 'Son of the Virgin' for ben ha-betulah — preserving the Hebrew title exactly as it appears. This is NOT 'Son of Man' (ben adam). The Hebrew author uses a Christological title rooted in Isaiah 7:14's virgin prophecy, not Daniel 7:13's 'one like a son of man.'
'In his light' for be-oro — the primordial light of Genesis 1:3, the light that precedes sun and moon.
textual_notes: Isaiah 7:14: 'Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: behold, the virgin (הבתולה) shall conceive and bear a son (בן), and shall call his name Immanuel.' The Hebrew title 'Son of the Virgin' directly combines Isaiah's הבתולה with the resulting בן — compressing the prophecy into a Christological title.

The presence of 'Son of the Virgin' where Greek has 'Son of Man' suggests the Hebrew tradition preserved an alternative or earlier Christological title. The Greek 'Son of Man' may reflect the Daniel 7 tradition while the Hebrew preserves the Isaiah 7 tradition.

chapter_notes.summary: Mark 8 in Hebrew contains two of the most extraordinary one-way markers in the entire Hebrew Gospels corpus. (1) שתי וערב ('warp and woof') in v34 where Greek has 'cross' — the Hebrew uses the Levitical weaving terminology from Leviticus 13 (the inspection of garments for impurity). The cross-shape is inherent in weaving (vertical warp crossed by horizontal woof), but NO back-translator from Greek σταυρός would independently generate this Levitical textile term. The connection to priestly purity examination adds a layer of meaning absent from the Roman execution instrument. (2) בן הבתולה ('Son of the Virgin') in v38 where Greek has 'Son of Man' — a completely different Christological title that directly invokes Isaiah 7:14 rather than Daniel 7:13. This is perhaps the single most theologically significant divergence between the Hebrew and Greek traditions in all of Mark. Additional strong markers include: חיל (host/army) for the crowd; שכנגדי ('my adversary') instead of 'Satan' for Keyfa; הפרד ('separate' — Pharisee root) as Yeshua's command to Keyfa; the כפר (deny/atone) wordplay; באורו ('in his light') vs. 'in glory'; האומה ('the nation') vs. 'the generation'; and verbatim quotation from Jeremiah 5:21 / Ezekiel 12:2 ('eyes and do not see, ears and do not hear'). The chapter builds to a climactic revelation: the one called Mashiach (v29) is also the Son of the Virgin (v38) — the Isaiah 7:14 prophecy fulfilled.
